もし あめ が ふったら — If it rains
You say “if / when” with ～たら, give advice with ～たら どう です か and pick up a topic with ～なら.
If it rains, let’s do it inside.
When you get home, call me.
If it’s the reception you mean, how about my place?
If it’s cheap, I’ll buy it.
To form ～たら from verbs (ふったら), adjectives (やすかったら, しずか だったら) and nouns (あめ だったら).
To tell “if” (a hypothesis) from “when” (certain): いえ に ついたら = when I get home.
To give advice with ～たら どう です か.
To use ～なら to pick up someone else’s topic.
Where shall we have the reception?
March. Ana and Mihai are eating ramen at Kenji’s and talking about the wedding: the ceremony is on 17 May at the town hall, but they still don’t have a place for the reception.
We’re having the ceremony at the town hall. But the place for the reception hasn’t been decided yet.
Restaurants are expensive, hotels seem cold…
If it’s the reception you mean, how about my place? I have a little garden at the back.
Really? But, Kenji, isn’t it too much for you?
Not at all. If it’s your wedding, I’ll do anything.
But what do we do if it rains?
If it rains, we’ll do it in the restaurant. …Ah, that’s a form you haven’t learned yet. We’ll do it inside.
(Laughing) Kenji, you talk like a teacher!
And what about the food? My mother says she wants to make sarmale, and Ana’s mother says she wants to make paella.
Good idea! If we have Spanish, Romanian and Japanese food, it’s perfect.
As for Japanese food, leave it to me. I’ll make ramen too.
Kenji… thank you so much. When I get home, I’ll call my mother right away.
if we do (a form from chapter 24)
The double pause (っ) carries over from the ～た form: fut-ta-ra, it-ta-ra, kat-ta-ra.
mo-shi: the “i” almost disappears: “mosh”. It goes at the start of the sentence, with a small pause after it.
dai-joh-bu: a long “o”; the final “u” almost silent.
Take the ～た form (chapter 16) and add ら. It works with every type of word:
The second half of the sentence can be in any tense (usually present / future) or a request: ～て ください, ～ましょう.
～たら has two meanings. Context tells you which:
If it rains, I won’t go. (a hypothesis)
When I get home, I’ll call you. (I’m sure to get home)
When spring comes, we’re getting married.
もし at the start strengthens the idea of a hypothesis (“if by any chance”). With もし, ～たら always means “if”.
3. Advice: ～たら どう です か
How about having a little rest? (casual)
It’s friendly advice. To a superior, it’s more polite to say: ～たら いかが です か (いかが = どう, polite).
～なら picks up what the other person said and adds a suggestion or information:
A: We don’t have a place for the reception. B: If it’s the reception you mean, how about my place?
As for Japanese food, leave it to me.
If you’re going to Kyoto anyway, see Kinkakuji.
The difference: ～たら = after X happens. ～なら = if X is true (even before it happens). きょうと に いく なら = if you’re planning to go (the advice is for BEFORE leaving).
“When I get home, I’ll call you.”
If it rains, I won’t go.
How about having a little rest?
Please call me when you get home.

しょうたいじょう — The invitation
The wedding invitation Ana and Mihai send to their Japanese friends.
Dear friends, we’re getting married on 17 May.
The ceremony will be at twelve noon, at Madrid town hall.
Afterwards we’re having the reception in the garden of Kenji’s restaurant.
If you can come, please let us know by the end of April.
We’d be very happy to see you. Mihai and Ana

ふたり の おかあさん — The two mothers
That evening, as soon as he got home, Mihai called his mother in Romania straight away.
“Mum, the place for the reception has been decided. It’s the garden of Kenji’s restaurant.”
Elena was overjoyed. But straight away she said this:
“If it’s in a garden, I’ll make a hundred sarmale and bring them.”
“A hundred? Mum, you can’t take them on the plane!”
“If I can’t take them on the plane, I’ll make them in Madrid. No problem.”
The next day, Ana’s mother, Carmen, came round.
Carmen had a big notebook. In it were written about a thousand ideas for the wedding.
“I’ll make the paella. If it’s a garden, I can make it in a big pan.”
Ana and Mihai looked at each other. A hundred sarmale and a giant pan of paella.
“I wonder if that much food will fit in Kenji’s restaurant…”
The food wasn’t the only problem.
Elena said: “For music, a Romanian hora would be good.”
Carmen said: “If there’s no sevillana, it isn’t a wedding.”
Elena: “The flowers should be white.” Carmen: “They should be red.”
Although they had never met, they already couldn’t agree on anything.
Mihai, in a fix, went to Kenji’s restaurant.
“Kenji, what do I do? If those two argue, the wedding will be ruined.”
Kenji listened calmly, stirring the ramen broth. Then he laughed.
“Mihai, don’t worry. How about getting them to cook together?”
“No problem. People who argue in the kitchen become friends in the kitchen. That’s how it was with my mother and grandmother too.”
At the end of April, Elena arrived in Madrid.
She had three suitcases. One with clothes, two with sauerkraut, minced meat and spices.
At the airport, Carmen and Elena met for the first time.
They had no language in common. Carmen didn’t know Romanian, and Elena didn’t know Spanish.
For a few moments they looked at each other in silence. Mihai and Ana didn’t even breathe.
Then Elena opened a suitcase and took out a little jar.
Inside was a handkerchief embroidered with a blue flower.
And Carmen took something out of her bag. It was a photo of an old white dress: the dress of Ana’s grandmother, Rosario.
They looked at the photo and the handkerchief and realised something.
If there were a blue flower on the bodice of the dress…
No words were needed. They smiled broadly and shook hands.
From that evening on, they stood together in the kitchen every day.
Elena showed how to roll sarmale, and Carmen how to use the flame for paella.
If they didn’t understand the words, they spoke with their hands. If they didn’t understand with their hands either, they tasted.
And when night fell, they secretly sewed the blue flower onto the dress together.
It was a secret from Ana. It was a secret from Mihai too.
A week later, Kenji dropped by and looked into the kitchen.
Elena and Carmen were laughing their heads off, making sarmale and paella.
“See? It’s just as I told you,” Kenji whispered to Mihai.
Mihai sighed with relief: “If it weren’t for you, Kenji, what would have become of me?”
Kenji thought for a moment, then answered: “You’d probably have eaten a hundred sarmale by yourself.”
That evening, Mihai said to Ana: “After the wedding is over, let’s give Kenji a thank-you present.”
Ana thought for a moment and smiled: “As for Kenji, I think there’s only one thing he wants.”
“What’s that?” “For Haruka and Sakura to come to Madrid.”
Mihai nodded. The invitation should already have arrived in Hiroshima.
